opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the hardest problems in the whole space. There are really two layers to it.

The first layer is the molecule itself: what does it actually smell like? That's the part we've made a lot of progress on. If you give me a chemical structure, can I predict whether people will describe it as fruity, woody, musky, green, and so on? That turns out to be learnable. You can train models, graph neural networks in our case, on structures paired with descriptions from trained panelists. Those models can predict odor character roughly as well as an individual human panelist does. So "what does this smell like" is becoming tractable.

"Does it smell *good*, and to *whom*" is a different and much messier question. Pleasantness, what scientists call hedonic valence, is partly baked into the biology. There are broad tendencies: most people find certain sulfur compounds repulsive and certain sweet or floral notes pleasant. But a huge amount of it is learned. It's culture, memory, and context. A note that reads as clean and fresh in one country might read as medicinal in another, because of what products it's been associated with there. Wintergreen is a classic example. In some places it's candy, and in others it's the smell of a pain-relief rub. Same molecule, totally different emotional response.

In practice, understanding a particular consumer means combining the two. You get a robust, objective description of what the scent *is*, then you layer on data about the people you care about: consumer panels, preference testing, and how different segments respond to different regions of that odor space. Once you have a good map of odors, you can ask much more precise questions. Instead of "do people like this perfume," you can ask "this group seems to gravitate toward this neighborhood of the map, so what else lives nearby that we haven't tried yet?"

So we don't try to predict "good" directly from the molecule. We first build a really good representation of smell, and then preference becomes something you can model on top of that, rather than a black box.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes whether a scent smells good from what it smells like, saying pleasantness depends on “to whom” and that the same molecule can prompt different emotional responses.

r002.rationale: It says preferences are largely learned through culture and memory, and gives product associations as a reason the same scent is perceived differently.

r003.rationale: It states that cultural and product context can change a scent’s emotional response, shaping whether it is experienced as pleasant or medicinal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually the hard part, right? Because when we say a scent smells "good," that's not one thing. There's a layer that's pretty universal, and then there's a layer that's incredibly personal and cultural.

The universal layer is more tractable than people think. If you take a molecule and ask a hundred people to rate it on pleasantness, there's actually a fair amount of agreement. Things that smell like rot, like decay, like sulfur compounds, almost everyone finds those unpleasant. Things that smell like fruit, like certain florals, there's a broad consensus that they're pleasant. And at Osmo, that was really one of the first things we wanted to see if a model could learn. Can you go from the structure of a molecule to a prediction of how a trained panel will describe it? And it turns out you can, and you can do it at or above the level of an individual human panelist, which was surprising to a lot of people in the field.

But then you get to the consumer layer, and here's where it gets interesting. Smell is wired into memory and emotion in a way that vision and hearing just aren't. The olfactory bulb has this very short path to the amygdala and the hippocampus. So whether you like a particular scent has a lot to do with what you've associated it with. If you grew up in a house where a certain cleaning product was used, that smell means "clean" to you. Somebody in another country, with a different product, has a completely different anchor for "clean." Fragrance houses know this. The same laundry detergent will be scented differently in Brazil versus Japan versus the US, because the expectations are different.

So the way I think about it is almost like two models stacked together. One is the physics and chemistry: molecule in, perceptual description out. The other is the context: who is this person, what are they expecting, what does this product category mean to them. The first one we're getting quite good at. The second one is really a question about people, and you need data about people to answer it, not just data about molecules.

And honestly, the thing I find most exciting is when you can close that loop. If you can predict what something will smell like before you make it, you can explore chemical space much more efficiently. You can say, I want something that reads as fresh and clean to this particular market, that's safe, that's biodegradable, that doesn't exist yet. And then go find candidate molecules that hit that target. That's the shift, from smell being this craft that lives in a perfumer's head to something you can actually search over.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes broadly shared pleasantness from a personal consumer layer, saying scent preference depends on the individual’s associations and expectations.

r002.rationale: It says prior associations shape whether someone likes a scent and gives an example based on growing up around a cleaning product.

r003.rationale: It states that smell is tied to memory and emotion and that these associations affect whether a person likes a scent.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two pieces to that. One is, what does this molecule or this mixture actually smell like? Is it floral, woody, smoky? The other is, do you like it? And those are related, but they’re not the same question.

Whether you like a smell depends a lot on your experiences and the context in which you encounter it. A smell might remind you of something your grandmother cooked, and that association makes it wonderful for you. Someone else might have a very different association with the same smell. And something that smells great in a food might not be what you want in a shampoo.

So you need to connect the chemistry to perception, and then connect perception to preference. You ask people to smell things and tell you what they perceive and what they like, and you look for patterns across those responses. The goal isn’t necessarily to find one scent that everybody loves. It’s to understand which scents work for which people, in which contexts.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes a scent’s smell from whether a particular person likes it and says preferences vary by person and context.

r002.rationale: It says liking depends a lot on personal experiences and illustrates how a remembered prior experience can make a scent appealing.

r003.rationale: It explains that encounter context affects liking, including an emotionally meaningful memory of a grandmother’s cooking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two pieces to that. One is, what does the molecule smell like? Is it floral, fruity, woody? The other is, what does that smell mean to you? And that second piece depends on your experiences, your culture, and the context in which you encounter it.

You might love a particular smell because it reminds you of something you ate growing up, while someone else has a completely different association. So predicting what something smells like is a starting point, but it doesn’t automatically tell you whether a particular consumer will like it.

To get at that, you need to connect the chemistry and the perceptual description with feedback from people. You have them smell things, tell you what they like, and look for patterns. The interesting question is how much of that preference generalizes across people, and how much you need to learn about the individual.

r001.rationale: The response says liking depends on what a smell means to a particular person and asks how much preference must be learned about the individual.

r002.rationale: It says meaning depends on a person’s experiences and gives a childhood food memory as an example shaping preference.

r003.rationale: It mentions the context in which someone encounters a scent, but does not clearly say that the person’s emotional context at that time shapes their preference.
